articles.title: Planet Money : NPR
articles.description: The U.S. is working on bringing back the ancient maritime practice of prize law — which allowed for privateers, or more recently, navies, to seize enemy-linked ships, and quickly sell them off. Why? Well, the U.S. has been seizing lots of big boats — oil tankers linked to Iran and Venezuela — in what the Pentagon calls an effort to disrupt ‘illicit networks.’ But after they seize the big boats, they have a big problem: Boats are very expensive to maintain, and each day the government owns them adds extra costs. So they want to sell off the tankers and the oil inside as soon as possible.On today’s show, pirates, some swashbuckling, and an interview with the federal judge tasked with standing up a modern-day prize court. Read: Our book: Planet Money: A Guide to the Economic Forces That Shape Your Life Our weekly longform Planet Money newsletterOur weekly Indicator round-up newsletterFollow: InstagramTikTokYouTubeFacebookSupport public media with NPR+ and enjoy perks for over 25 podcasts like this one. This show’s perks include bonus episodes and sponsor-free listening. Learn more at plus.npr.org.This episode of Planet Money was hosted by Nick Fountain. It was produced by Sam Yellowhorse Kesler. It was edited by Marianne McCune. It was fact-checked by Sierra Juarez, engineered by Robert Rodriguez and Jimmy Keeley. Alex Goldmark is Planet Money's executive producer.

articles.title: Pakistan Internet Outage: Did Iran Target Subsea Cables? | Vantage
articles.description:
Did Iran cut Pakistan's internet cables? Internet services across parts of Pakistan were disrupted after a fault was reported in the SMW5 international submarine cable system, around 11 kilometres off Pakistan's coast. Pakistan's Telecommunications Authority (PTA) says the cause of the fault remains unknown, and there is no evidence linking Iran to the incident.
However, the outage comes amid growing concerns over Iran's threats to target undersea internet cables in the Persian Gulf if the United States and Israel launch fresh military strikes against Tehran.
In October 2026, Iranian officials warned that critical submarine communications cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz could become targets.
So, could undersea internet infrastructure become the next front in the Iran conflict? And if Iran were to target Pakistan, would it have a reason?
Pakistan and Iran may describe each other as brotherly neighbours, but their relationship has been marked by border tensions, cross-border militancy and the January 2024 exchange of missile strikes. Hem Kaur Saroya tells you more on Vantage on Firstpost.
